<p>The first few weeks after birth are a marathon of sleeplessness, diaper changes, and breastfeeding. Amidst this chaos, a thought suddenly occurs to you: <em>"My period hasn't returned yet. Is this normal?"</em>.</p><p>For some women, the absence of a period is a great relief (no extra hygiene issues!), while for others, it is a source of concern ("Could I be pregnant again?").</p><p>The truth is that the restoration of the postpartum cycle is different for every woman and depends mainly on one factor: <strong>How are you feeding your baby?</strong></p><p>In this article, we will explain how the process works for breastfeeding and non-breastfeeding mothers, how true the "breastfeeding protects" myth is, and how the first period will differ from previous ones.</p><h2>Lochia (Postpartum Bleeding) or Period?</h2><p>First of all, it is necessary to distinguish between these two concepts. The bleeding that begins immediately after birth and lasts up to 4-6 weeks is not a period, but <strong>Lochia</strong>. This is the process of the uterus cleaning and restoring itself.</p><ul><li><p>Bleeding stops after lochia ends. If bleeding starts again after some time, it may already be the first period.</p></li></ul><h2>Scenario 1: Exclusively Breastfeeding Mothers</h2><p>If you are <strong>exclusively</strong> breastfeeding your baby (without giving water, supplementary food, or formula) frequently both day and night, the arrival of your period may be significantly delayed.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Reason:</strong> The hormone <strong>Prolactin</strong> secreted during breastfeeding suppresses ovulation. If there is no ovulation, there is no period. In medicine, this is called <strong>Lactational Amenorrhea</strong>.</p></li><li><p><strong>Duration:</strong> A period may not occur for 6 months to 1 year (sometimes until breastfeeding ends).</p></li><li><p><strong>Note:</strong> As soon as the baby starts supplementary food or night feedings decrease, prolactin levels drop and the cycle is restored.</p></li></ul><h2>Scenario 2: Mothers Using Formula</h2><p>If your baby is fed with formula or if you are not breastfeeding, your body exits "pregnancy mode" and returns to its normal routine much faster.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Duration:</strong> The period is usually restored <strong>6-8 weeks after birth</strong> (approximately 1.5 - 2 months).</p></li><li><p>If there is still no period after 3 months, it is recommended to consult your doctor.</p></li></ul><h2>Scenario 3: Mixed Feeding (Breast Milk + Formula)</h2><p>In this case, it is difficult to give a prognosis. The period may start 2-3 months after birth or even later. Everything depends on the frequency of breastfeeding.</p><h2>What Will the First Period Be Like? (Changes)</h2><p>The first period after birth may not be like it was before pregnancy. Your body is not yet fully balanced hormonally.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Bleeding:</strong> It may be heavier or lighter. The presence of small clots is normal.</p></li><li><p><strong>Pain:</strong> Good news! Many women—especially those who suffered from pain due to endometriosis—report that period cramps significantly <strong>decreased</strong> or completely disappeared after birth. The reason is the expansion of the uterus and hormonal changes.</p></li><li><p><strong>Regularity:</strong> The cycle may be irregular for the first few months. It will settle over time.</p></li></ul><h2>The "Breastfeeding Protects" Myth and Pregnancy Risk</h2><p>The biggest danger lies here. Many women think that if their period hasn't returned, they cannot get pregnant. <strong>WRONG!</strong></p><ul><li><p><strong>Mechanism:</strong> <strong>Ovulation</strong> occurs approximately 2 weeks before menstrual bleeding. That is, you can ovulate and get pregnant before you even see the first drop of blood.</p></li><li><p><strong>Result:</strong> Relaxing and thinking "breast milk protects me" can result in an unplanned "surprise" pregnancy.</p></li></ul><h3>When does the Lactational Amenorrhea Method (LAM) protect you?</h3><p>For this method to be 98% effective, 3 conditions <strong>must</strong> be met:</p><ol><li><p>The baby is less than 6 months old.</p></li><li><p>Your period has not yet returned.</p></li><li><p>The baby <strong>only</strong> eats breast milk (day and night, every 4 hours).</p></li></ol><p>If one of these conditions is violated or if you do not want to take a risk, talk to your doctor about <strong>contraception</strong> (IUD, condoms, or "mini-pills" suitable for breastfeeding mothers) 4-6 weeks after birth.</p><h2>Does it Affect Milk Supply?</h2><p>When the period is restored, some mothers may notice a temporary decrease in milk supply. This is related to hormonal changes.</p><ul><li><p><strong>Does the taste change?</strong> The taste of the milk may be slightly salty, and the baby may be fussy about nursing for a few days. Be patient; this is temporary.</p></li></ul><h2>Summary</h2><p>The postpartum period is your body's way of saying, "I have recovered and am ready to be a mother again." Whether this happens 2 months or 1 year later—both cases are normal.</p><p>The main point is to protect yourself during this period and be ready for surprises.</p><p>To track your cycle and not miss ovulation days, download the <strong>"Anacan" app</strong>. Our app works with a special algorithm for breastfeeding mothers!</p>
